line: # legend: [yogh] a reversed/tailed "3" shape resembling a script z or yogh (ʒ), often word-initial.
# legend: [eps] a backward-C / epsilon shape (ε), sometimes with a short horizontal bar through the opening.
# legend: [theta] a small circle bisected by a horizontal bar (θ); frequently doubled (θθ) at line/segment openings.
# legend: [omega] a rounded arch or horseshoe shape open at the bottom (Ω), sometimes sitting on a short underbar.
# legend: [rho] a p-like letter whose descender curls back into a full loop to the left (ρ).
# legend: [boxbar] a small square or rectangle enclosing a vertical or cross stroke (looks like a boxed H or ⊞).
# legend: [chibar] an X-shape crossed by an extra short diagonal or horizontal tick, distinct from a plain unmarked "x".
# legend: [eqbar] two short parallel horizontal strokes stacked, like "=".
# legend: [dash] an isolated short horizontal stroke used as its own glyph between other symbols (not a hyphen joining letters).
# legend: [tilde2] two small stacked wavy horizontal squiggles, drawn as a free-standing glyph (resembles a doubled nasal tilde or sideways "m").
# legend: [cross] a small "+" or dagger-like mark standing alone as a glyph.

# legend: [loopdesc] a letter-like shape with an extra descending or looping tail that does not match an ordinary Latin letterform (e.g. an over-elaborated d/g/8 shape); used for several distinct but similarly-elaborated shapes, see notes.
# legend: [bar-above] a straight horizontal stroke drawn over a base symbol (combining mark; written as base+[bar-above]).
# legend: [dot-above] a single dot drawn over a base symbol (combining mark; written as base+[dot-above]).
# legend: [hook] a small hook or comma-like flourish attached to the side of a base symbol, read as an addition to it.

# note: This is a single-pass, moderate-confidence reading. The cipher hand mixes invented symbols with reused Latin letters and digits at small size with faint, uneven ink; several shapes coded here as [loopdesc] are NOT necessarily the same glyph as each other (elaborated d/g/8-like forms recur but with visibly different loop placement) and should be split into distinct codes once compared against passA and higher-resolution originals.

# note: f277r_L1 s1-s2 and f277r_L4 s2-s3, f277r_L8 s3-s4, f277r_B1 s1, f277r_C1 s2 (part), f277r_C2 s4, and f277v_L1 s1-s2 were read as ordinary English cursive (plaintext), but the hand is difficult secretary/mixed cursive and many letters inside those [PLAIN:...] tokens are marked "?"; these stretches need a second, careful look, ideally at higher zoom.

# note: f277r_C2 s1-s2 contains a stretch that appears struck through (crossed by horizontal pen strokes) before a plaintext phrase resembling "...vnto ...proof/cryptograph..."; the [struck] tag was applied to that group, but the exact extent of the strike (which tokens it covers) is uncertain.

# note: The dash-like tokens transcribed as [dash] between letters/symbols (e.g. "o [dash] o [dash] [omega]") may instead be a single connecting flourish/ligature rather than three separate glyphs; treat with caution.

# note: Segment overlaps (~10%) were used to align repeated symbols at segment boundaries (e.g. [omega] shared between L1 s3 end and s4 start; [theta][theta] shared between L2 s1/L3 s1 line openings), but exact token-for-token boundary alignment was not independently re-verified pixel by pixel.

# note: Greek-letter-like shapes (theta, epsilon, rho, omega, gamma) are treated here as invented cipher symbols (bracket-coded) rather than "ordinary letters," per the instruction that only standard Latin letters/digits are written as themselves; this choice should be revisited if the reconciler judges them to be actual Greek letters used as such.
